tasks.desc: Ideation: formulate tile orientations as XOR constraints and choose parity DSU

Implement the cell-state parity DSU solver: A cells get variables P (N/S) and Q (E/W), B cells get one variable R; store hvar/vvar and flip (1 for A, 0 for B); for each horizontal torus edge k->right unite hvar[k] with hvar[right] using constant flip[k], and for each vertical torus edge k->down unite vvar[k] with vvar[down] using constant flip[k]; output 0 on contradiction, otherwise pow(2, component_count, 998244353)
Validate with brute force on tiny random grids (including H=2/W=2 and all-A odd cycle cases) and the sample
If validation fails, implement dual edge-state XOR system as an independent cross-check/fallback
Finalize fast I/O and memory-efficient implementation for total HW 1e6 and T up to 1e5

proposals: Implement the cell-state XOR system with a weighted/parity union-find as the primary approach: Type-A cells get two variables, Type-B cells get one, and every horizontal/vertical torus adjacency gives one XOR equation.

Implement the dual edge-state XOR system as an independent cross-check: one variable per grid edge midpoint, with local parity constraints per cell, especially checking that Type-B cells impose all required constraints.

Try a signed two-layer graph propagation version: create vertical and horizontal port nodes, identify the two ports for Type-B cells, add signed adjacency edges, and count balanced components by BFS/DFS or parity DSU.
Consider sparse GF(2) linear algebra only as a fallback or verification method, being careful about memory and fill-in; it is less natural than pairwise parity constraints.
Use transfer-matrix or tensor-network contraction only for very small width/height sanity checks, not as the main solution, because the state space is exponential in the smaller dimension.
Explore loop/homology/FKT-style interpretations only as a theoretical alternative, since torus global cycles and model mapping are subtle and likely overkill.
Validate any implementation on tiny random grids by brute force, paying special attention to H=2 or W=2 cases where the torus has parallel edges.
